NATARAJAN I Communist China, little thought has been given to the objectives of the Government of India. But, as Goethe put it, life is not light but its refracted rays, and more can be found out by the reactions of Mr, Nehru to events than by the actual actions of his Government. This is parti- cularly true of three different directions from which moves have taken place to restore peace, security and freedom from sudden attack or the threat of it, to India. ie the midst of much speculation about the policy and purposes of The first of these and the most energetic has come from the West with the U.S.A. and Britain playing a leading role. While keeping strictly to the atttitude of not disturbing India’s foreign policy, Mr. Averell Harriman and Mr. Duncan Sandys have exerted themselves energetically | to bring India and Pakistan together to try to settle under pressure out- standing problems which have eluded solution for fifteen years. That their efforts have left an impression must be inferred from the quiet talks going on between officials of the two countries rather than from the public postures adopted the politicians and the press. The suggestion that the defence of the sub-continent can only be effective if India and Pakistan get together, provoked an angry reaction in India where it is taken to mean the exercise of pressure on the Government to make unreasonable concessions to Pakistan. There is too an apprehension that it ls a manceuvre to align India by drawing her into the framework of Western military alliances, while appearing to ignore and even welcome the Indian Government’s expectations of, and efforts to secure, assistance from Soviet Russia. The second is the Colombo effort of the six non-aligned countries from Asia and Africa, The decisions of the Conference have not been officially released but press reports suggest that the compromise proposed is not acceptable to India. Mr. Nehru himself, before he received the proposal, commented wrily that others do not see things the way India does, and, afterwards, replied to an old letter from North Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh categorically asserting that he could accept no modification of his demand for withdrawal of Chinese forces to the pre-September 8, 1962 boundaries as a pre-condition for Sino-Indian talks. Further, he has indicated to Mrs. Bandarnaike that other engagements prevent him from

Mrs. Bandarnaike too who opened the Colombo Conference with a fervent plea for quick action, has shown little anxiety to complete the mission with despatch. , The third effort relates to Soviet Russia’s attitude and its position in the Communist world vis-a-vis China. President Kardelj of Yugo- slavia who was with Marshal Tito during recent talks with Mr. Khrushchev, is at present in India and will no doubt throw some light on the quarrels between Russia and China which have of late received considerable pub- licity. Without meaning more than to utter a warning, it mght be pointed out that Mr. Khrushchev and Marshal Tito have their own peace to patch up, and that once before, when Hungary’s freedom was lost, Mr. Nehru was misled by Marshal Tito’s advice. It is difficult to say in such cases how far Yugoslavia’s attitude is influenced by ideological considerations and how much of it springs from misreading on the basis of inadequate knowledge. A direct message from Mr. Khrushchev would noturally be better than an interpretation by Mr. Kardelj. Mr. Nehru has indicated often enough that he does not expect more from Russia than ‘neutrality’ and token help. In international politics one usually does not obtain more than one looks for. Consequently, Soviet Russia has been the slowest to move, unimpressed by any idea of urgency. Now that the Prime Minister has lost his diplomatic innocence, it is useful to note that Russia might well find her purpose served by seeing China involved in protracted trouble in South Asia, using her influence with the Indian Government just sufficiently to bring about a limitation of aid from the West to the requisite amount. Much useful information on this tech- nique can be gleaned from Milovan Djilas’ “Conversations with Stalin” where the strategy of Communist States in fostering the natural suspi- cions of non-aligned nations about the West is depicted boldly. To the fear that the non-alignment policy is endangered by the prompt help extended by the West, the Prime Minister apparently adds a genuine anxiety lest in domestic affairs all this might bring about a swing to the “Right”, in the Government, the Congress and the country. His sharp reaction to any criticism from the Swatantra Party, his eager white- washing of Indian Communists, and his ascribing Chinese aggression to ‘Han imperialism’ rather than Communism are significant pointers to his mind. We are now at a stage when, in his own interest, it is necessary that these fears should be allayed ; it is, of course, important for the country’s future that they should not be exploited as they so easily could be. Mr. Nehru, however, has no need to fear the increasing influence of the Right—in fact, he has every reason to rethink for himself whether the terms ‘Leftism’ and ‘Rigtism’ have any meaning in the Indian or inter- national context. For one thing, he has admitted that for all his Govern- ment’s emphasis on Socialism, the poor have been badly served by the two Five-Year Plans while the rich have thriven. Moreover, under war conditions the Government has ample powers which it could exercise

As a matter of fact, twelve economists of New Delhi published a statement in the Press asking the Government _ to introduce a supplementary budget in early December—“the logical opportunity for it exists and such a budget would have fulfilled a visible need and made concrete, for many, the conception of ‘sacrifice’, Delhi’s response was that the regular budget would come in three months’ time, and “where is the hurry and why not wait until the magnitude of. the financial resources necessary is clearly determined.” Internati . it is very fitting to recall Djilas’ report of Stalin’s admission that there are ways other than Communism to Socialism, citing particularly Britain's achievements. Thus neither in the domestic sphere nor in international affairs is there any reasonable ground for fearing any greater pressure from conservative elements than has existed so far. On the contr, % there is every reason to feel confident that wisely handled the present crisis would afford an opportunity to correct past mistakes and place eco- nomic development on a sound footing. For this, the urgent requirement is to give the Government’s policies greater purpose and direction, 0 The Kashmir involvement presents the major obstacle in a settlement with Pakistan, though it is open to question whether agreement over Kashmir will end the differences which extend over wider questions. I was strongly for effecting a merger of Jammu and Kashmir with India on a basis which ensures the extension of democratic institutions and good government to that State. Moreover, there have been oppor- tunities to achieve this without outraging world opinion and we have failed to take advantage of them for two reasons: Firstly, Mr. Nehru’s insistence on a plebiscite has led us to ignore the many evidences of the ruling party’s willingness to merge; secondly, there have been more than one instance of the United Nations conceding the substance of our claim but our concern to get the letter of its as well pre- vented our making progress in Kashmir affairs, As a result of these failures, we have been driven back to stalemate along the cease-fire line, to acrimonious argument with Pakistan and to support of undemocratic practices within the State. We might excuse Sheikh Abdullah’s prolonged detention but it is difficult to justify it. It is little consolation that in the Pakistan-held area of Kashmir far worse conditions prevail. While political conditions prevailing in Pakistan are reflected in Pakistani Kashmir, those obtaining in India do not manifest themselves in Jammu and Kashmir. There is nothing new in the idea of the defence of the sub-continent being an integrated enterprise. It was this that formed the basis of the interest in keeping India entire, and, if the military consideration was not in the minds of the politicians, it was nonetheless a reality. Asa matter of fact, the original intention was to arrange for joint defence even after the agreement to partition. It was not the Government of India

That it should be revived after the Chinese attacks of October by U.S. and British representatives interested in rendering effective help to India was to be expected. More- over, any scheme of long-term aid to India to build up her defences must mean some dovetailing into the system of military alliances already worked out by the West. It has often been suggested by American political writers that the nations in Asia which have accepted the democratic life, ought to assume greater responsibility for maintaining it against threats in this region. But, though this is the very sentiment Mr. Nehru gives expression to when he regrets the failure of some democratic neighbours to support India or accepts military help from the West, India has always leant heavily on her non-alignment policy not only to keep out of involvement but sometimes even to play a leading role in bringing about cease-fire arrange- ments which have worked to the advantage of the Communists who alter- nate negotiation and aggression to gain their ends. In so far as India continues to hold to non-alignment, we must expect indifference and even opportunism to govern the policies of other Asian countries. In this context, the Kashmir question is of practically little importance. India will have to consider the future of Kashmir more from the point of conditions now obtaining there than from that of holding or ceding territory. There have been petitions and statements complaining about the administration but much of their contents cannot be proved. What is an incontrovertible fact is that constitutional changes have taken place and the way elections were conducted in 1962 proves the instability of the system. Up to 1962, the Kashmir Legislative Assembly's 75 seats were not all filled—some 25 seats were held in abeyance pending recovery of territory from Pakistan and providing representation for peoples of that area. The 1962 elections, for the first time, saw all the 75 seats filled with no reference to members from the Pakistan-held areas of K What was more, the ruling party secured 67 of the seats—a |. of them being filled by uncontested returns. The phenomenon h generally explained as due to Kashmir’s first introduction to parlian democracy. But this form of election has not much to commen Obviously, the existing arrangements are not in the least satisf Among the features that need correction are the special arrangement made for Kashmir State—as, for example, the designation Minister for the chief executive, and a semi-permanent head of § which are outward signs of the discrimination that is Kashmir. A « fire—we are beginning to appreciate it now that the Chinese have fc it on us—is a temporary expedient. But after World War II it ha come a means of holding the status quo between two nations and the conflicting clams. A throughly unsatisfactory arrangement so far t people residing in the disputed territory who are subjected to a prolo period of uncertainty and instability, it should be the interest of all , to bring it to an end as soon as possible. There is no reason why lh should resent the fact that she has to do under the compulsion of an aggressive enemy that which should have been done long ago. We must of Pi

Nor should we ignore the fact that had such accession taken place, China could not have en- croached into Ladakh without becoming involved in hostilities with the Western powers since Pakistan is part of the military system built up by the West. In a recent issue of the Economist, it was darkly stated that the State of Jammu and Kashmir which had been divided between two nations so far, would be in future be divided between three. This surely is a state of affairs which, in the interests of the people of Kashmir, must be sought strenously to be ended. So order is issued that any person who touches Humpty Dumpty even with his finger- tips be cast into the dungeon, ¥ No other interpretation can be put on the various announcements made lately by government and quasi-government spokesmen that all those who criticise the government, and particularly the Prime Minister, are liable to be arrested under the Defence of India Act. That this is no mere threat is borne out by the recent arrests of Messers Dharmapa, Roop Narain and N. N. Datta, the three signatories of a memorandum widely circulated among members of Parliament criticising the policy of the government and asking for Nehru’s removal. The three are associated with the Committee Against Chinese Aggression and the Afro-Asian Council ! This attitude adopted by politicians in power poses a serious threat to the freedom of citizens to express their views on the acts of the government in the present state of emergency. If we only examine the political philosophy underlying democracy, it will become clear that such thinking is opposed to its basic tenets. One of the main grounds on which democracy is preferred to dictator- ship or oligarchy is that it allows an individual the maximum degree of freedom, the paramount freedom being the freedom to change the men who are in control of the affairs of the nation. A compromise of course has to be made between this freedom to demand and procure a change in the government and the safety and efficient running of the State. That is why laws impose certain restrictions on this right. Take the law of sedition, for instance. Under Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code, “whoever by words . . . or otherwise brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite dis- affection to Is the government established by law in India, shall be pt th imprisonment for life... . : The expression ‘disaffection’ includes disloyalty and on 2; Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means lout exciting or attempting to excite hatred, contempt or disaffection, constitute an offence under this Section. Explanation 3: Comments expressing disapprobation of the admi- nistrative or other action of the government without exciting or attempting to excite hatred, contempt or disaffection, do not constitute an offence under this ction.” Explanations 2 and 3 clearly imply that an individual is free to cri- ticize the goyernment and to demand a change of government,

\ J OPINION, December 25, 1962 People forget that the word “government” is often loosely used to connote two different things, viz., the existing political system and a parti- cular set of ministers. A particular set of ministers may be open to objections. To assail them and even to excite hatred against them is not to excite hatred against the government. It would only infringe the law of libel. It is a well-settled law that it is not sedition to seek change of a government by constitutional means in order that another govern- ment equally constitutional may be substituted in its place in a consti- tutional way. It is sedition only if an attempt is made to unlawfully over- The relevant provisions of the Defence of India Act and Rules do not materially affect this legal position because the words used are very similar. Rule 35(6) (e) lays down that “ ‘Prejudicial act’ means any act which is intended or is likely to bring into hatred or contempt, or to excite disaffection towards the government established by law in India” —a simplified version of Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code. It should be noted that the purpose of explanations under that Section is to clarify the words used in the Section and not to add to their meaning. So that the absence of any explanations under Rule 35(6) (e) of the Defence of India Rules does not in any way widen the scope of the words used there. The question is: Does the existence of a state of emergency make any difference to the freedom of the individual to demand a new govern- ment? It is true that in an emergency more and more varied measures may be necessary to ensure the safety of the State. It may be necessary, for instance, to take speedy measures to meet a changing situation so that discussions for the cultivation of public support may have to be abandoned. But it can never be, that even in an emergency, the people cannot change their ministers if they think that they are taking wrong decisions which prejudice the safety and prestige of the nation. For, that is the very essence of democracy distinguishing it form dictatorship. A striking illustration of this principle is the motion placed before the British Parliament in the name of Sir John Wardlaw-Milne (an influ ential member of the Conservative Party) on 25th June 1952 during critical period of the Second World War. OPINION, December 25, 1962 EC eer acceptance of the existence of more than a dozen national languages and their regional boundaries. ‘Linguisim’ and ‘provincialism’ are two words of abuse coined to belittle these sentiments. If the existence of national languages and their regional spread are accepted, it should not be diffi- cult to demarcate the boundaries. General principles can be laid down and all boundaries demarcated without fear or favour with the help of the leaders of different States. It is wrong to think that the existence of linguistic provinces would undermine the unity of India. A proof of the strong patriotic feeling of people speaking all languages has been given recently when China attack- ed India, In fact, this upsurge of peoples’ feelings has been the only un- equivocal non-confused reaction of the past months. Our leaders who did not suffer from languism and provincialism were the most confused in the hour of crisis, The communist ideology divided smaller countries like Korea and Viet-nam into two sections. Perhaps, the Chinese hoped to do that in India but the patriotism of the unsophisticated multi-lingual, multi-religious, multi-cultural masses has frustrated this attempt. People of one language wish to come together because they can learn in their own language and communicate easily with others, and the linguistic Tegion happens to be also the region within which over ninety percent of marriages take place. To ignore this wish and abuse those who have it does not help Indian unity. Clarity and sense of justice are needed also in the issues about public and private enterprise, socialism, agricultural policy and moralistic nega- tive laws like prohibition which have brought in more serious moral crime than drinking ever did. The present confusion is, on the one side, due to unthinking imitation of certain slogans and certain ideologies of the West, and, on the other, blindness to history with a curious conviction of the spiritual superiority of Indians over others. Talk of socialism with definite leanings towards communism is part of this imitative behaviour, Socialism and communism have functioned long enough in the West for us to analyse their social effects. The cruel r techniques of the communist regime are historical data now. and fair play, coupled with regard for human life, cannot be re- ciled with communist practices. All the communist political leaders and power holders, all their scientists and military personnel are no more working people than anywhere else in the world. The process of liquidation of opponents in a communist regime is so fearful that, if for nothing else, just for this one cruelty communism should be suspect. History has taught us the bitter lesson that being governed by others is not good in any way. But our leaders have failed to learn this lesson thoroughly. They have failed to notice that the communist nations of today hold down other nations, and their rule is neither less cruel nor less rigorous than that of the worst imperialists or capitalists. The same type of exploitation of men and material is found in both. For instance, full internal self-government involved the replacement of the three official ministers yet in the Executive Council (the Chief Secretary, the Attorney- General and the Finance Minister) ; but the British Government pleaded for the retention of the official Finance Minister for some time because Britain has been meeting the deficit on the budget of about £ 1.5 million a year, since Nyasaland, because of its opposition to federation, refuses to avail itself of the subvention it used to receive from the Federal budget, estimated at between £2.5 and £4 millions annually. Britain is also contributing £3 millions to Nyasaland’s development plan. So long as such assistance is imperatively required, it is natural that some amount of British control should continue. Dr. Banda saw the reasonableness of the plea. The new constitution thus provides that normally the Governor will consult the Cabinet in exercising his functions and act on its advice “except where he considers it necessary for the purpose of discharging his responsibility . . . for the purpose of maintaining financial and econo- mic stability.” Accordingly, the Governor will have power to veto finan- cial measurers or to introduce measures of his own under the new constitu- tion. Similarly, there will have to be reservations in the legislative field. The constitution has to be framed on the basis that Nyasaland is for the time being a member of the Central African Federation though it hopes to secede on the attainment of independence, and certain functions of the territorial government will be carried out by the Federal Government in Salisbury. For this reason under the new constitution the Governor will have to be authorized to exercise without consultation of the Cabinet “functions in relation to matters not within the constitutional competance of the Nyasaland Government.” The Governor will accordingly have power to veto in part or whole amy legislation which would exceed the competance of the territorial Government. In the closing s ssion of the conference two topics were dominant : future role of expatriate civil servants and the safeguards for the » settlers and other minority groups. It is normal to introduce a ation s at the stage of full self-government when the pecial transitional powers are withdrawn, Such a scheme ore be worked out later with the co-operation of the Malawi Congress party, which fully realizes the justice of the use of the transi- tional powers designed to delay any hasty withdrawals or early preoccu- pation with lump sum compensation. A Bill of Rights, based largely on the Uganda precedent, will be incorporated in the constitution in the interest of racial and other minorities. It will guarantee personal liberty, freedom of conscience, expression and assembly, protection of privacy of the home, and protection from deprivation of property without compen- sation. Reason, thought, sensitivity have nothing to do with our treatment of the cow, The only relevant factor in our attitude is habit. The fear of thinking, and of taking the further step of expressing our thoughts has become second nature to us. Why is it that we cannot and indeed do not wish to think? Is it because of centuries of repressive political rule? Is it because thinking has always been the job of the priests, the pundits and the moulvis and theré is no point in each one thinking for himself anyway? Or is it that we have adopted the princi- ple of the young Tory lad who assured his father that he would never join the Labour party because “I will never think” ? Whatever the reason Naipaul is absolutely right when he says that no event, whether strange or familiar, ever produces in us an effort to speculate or to reason. Our very gossip is nothing but a retailing, without comment, of facts heard at second hand. “It is a unique type of gossip. How can it be described? It is unslanted. It states facts and draws no conclusions.” There is no linking together, no interpretation, no personal beliefs or opinions which develop or grow out of these facts. to office through the free choice of his people, or assumes power by force, both in character and in impact, A nation which seeks to lead other 20 OPINION, February 23, 1965 leader within his own nation-state, no matter how strenuous or even dangerous his tasks may be, has the advantage of knowing at first-hand the problems and aspirations of his fellow-citizens. Whether he is elected he is given, or claims to have a mandate from his fellow-citizens—or, as the Chinese put it more dramatically, a “mandate from heaven.” If he fails to satisfy his people, he sooner or later loses his mandate, either by defeat at the polls, or by forceful overthrow of his regime. In either case, while his removal from the scene may have repercussions outside his own country, particularly in our age of jet planes and Telstar com- munications, the most immediate impact is made on his own people. ~ But the problems of leadership in world affairs are far different, nations—either in defending them against actual or potential foes, as for example in South Vietnam, or in their economic and social develop- ment, as the United States is doing today for some 90 countries—assumes an exceptional responsibility. For this responsibility concerns not only its own security and development, but the kind of leadership which the United States had avoided from the founding of the Republic until World War I, and undertook, only with great reluctance, after World War II, from which other great powers had emerged gravely weakened by war- time destruction. For, let us recall—strange as,it may seem today—that for nearly 150 years the United’ States, at the bidding of President | George Washington, foreswore all entangling alliances, and was, in effect, | what we today call a non-aligned nation. < What should acceptance of leadersh‘p in world affairs mean for the United States? It should mean three important things. First, it means a determination to understand the ever-changing world situation at any given time as clearly, and deal with it as dispassionately, as possible. Nothing could be more dangerous for a great power like the United States than to look at the world “through a glass darkly”—a glass obscured by prejudice, fear, or lack of impartial information about other peoples of the world. These three obscuring factors, to give an important example, have long affected American judgment of events in the US.S.R. \ and in China. They led to a policy of non-recognition of the Soviet gov- ernment for 16 years, and of Peking, so far, for 14 years—contrary to international law, which prescribes that a government, whatever its origin or character, should be recognized when it is in control of the territory of the state over which rules. Knowledge of the circumstances which to the two great revolutions of our times—in Russia and China—distas ful as we may find them, would have enabled us to pass informed judg- ment on those events with a sense of historical perspective which is too often absent from the making of foreign policy, particularly when policy is adjusted to meet what is believed to be public opinion. ep There is no doubt whatever that public opinion must be taken into consideration in a democracy like the United States. But here comes the

OPINION, February 23, 1965 a second important aspect of world affairs leadership. What is Public opinion ? It is particularly important that, in a democracy, public opinion should be not the result of ignorance or passion, but of accurate informa- tion dispassionately obtained and considered. To achieve this end, we owe it to ourselves, as well as to the rest of the world, to make certain that our citizens obtain impartial information about world affairs—and obtain it not only in our colleges and universities where instruction on this sub- ject is rapidly expanding, yet which only a small percentage of our citizens attend, but, far more important, in our elementary and high schools, where the majority of Americans—and this also means of our voters—receive their terminal education. A democratic government, for its part, must listen carefully, without fear or favour, to what we poetically call “the voice of the people”, and this means of the entire people—not merely the voice of special pleaders or organized lobbies, as was long done in the case of the China Lobby which Opposed recognition of Peking. In the final count, it is the Presi- dent must decide between possible alternative courses, and take the res- ponsibility for his decision. And, third, and most important in dealing with world affairs, we must take into consideration not only the interests of the United States, which understandably come first, as is true of all nations, but also the interests —and thus the feelingi—cf peoples outside our borders. There was a time when great powers thought of themselves as benefactors of the inhabitants of Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America—regarded by the West as inferior—whose territories they acquired, whose resources th utilized for their own economic development, and whose ports and cities they used for strategic purposes. This was the policy which the British immortalized by the phrase ‘white man’s burden.” And there is no doubt that many of the tasks at one time performed by white men overseas were useful to the peoples they ruled. But the days of the “white man’s burden” are over. They are over in considerable part because Americans—descendants of immigrants from other lands—who first came here as colonists from Britain and France, rose up against Britain’s rule, and from that time on-unalterably opposed the colonialism of Western European nations, as they now oppose colonialism by the U.S.S.R. and China. Thus Americans effectively aided the dissolution of colonial empires after World War II. Yet today we do not always understand that some of our own policies, no matter how well-intentioned, appear to others as tinged not only by self-interest—this is normal behaviour for all nations—but by colonial attitudes, notably in Latin America. And in South Vietnam, where the United States has acted alone, with little or no consultation either with yur allies or with the United Nations, we have found ourselves shoulder- ing the white man’s burden—but in a post-colonial period, when this role is no longer acceptable to others, and therefore not workable for the United States. |

OPINION, February 23, 1965 * The essence of leadership in world affairs is to recognize not only the potentialities, but also the limits, of such leadership, and the need, in our age, when great powers can no longer dominate the scene, of working with other nations, to create conditions under which all can work effect- ively—not only for the good of the rich and the powerful, as in the past, but of all peoples, however poor and weak. That the temper of 1965 runs to a more modest appraisal of the leader- ship of the United States in world affairs than has been made in the past twenty years is indicated by the comment of the dean of American com- mentators, Walter Lippmann, long known for his interest in constructive foreign policy, who on February 2 wrote favourably about President Johnson’s concern for domestic reforms, adding: “The time has come to stop beating our heads against stone walls under the illusion that we have been appointed policemen to the human race.” In short, the problem of leadership i world affairs, as in domestic affairs, is to forge the Great Society of the future, which the United Nations, however limited its present capacity to act, is constantly striving to achieve. For today our best hope of making our leadership acceptable to other peoples, all of whom think in terms of their interests, like ourselves, is not to impose it upon others—but only offer it to’ thdse who wish to accept it, yet have no desire to become our supine and unquestioning followers, As Vice-President Hubert H. Humphrey said at the opening of the im- pressive Nehru exhibition in New York on January 27, the United States feels it has an unwritten alliance with India—an alliance based not on specific pledges, but on the values the two nations share: “the rule of law, free elections, the checks and balances of a written constitution, a belief in the integrity of the individual, a desire for extending the benefits of modern society to all.” Between nations, as between individuals, the strongest bonds are not those which are forged by military power or by money. Let us practice what the young lovers in the American musical No Strings tell each other : No strings—no strings at all Except our own devotion No other bonds at all.

She took no notice and was often cheeky. The Indian woman, who was a friend of the other, followed her example except that instead of cheek she became abjectly humble and shed tears. Menon had no direct contact with these women; he hardly knew their names. He had no basis whatsoever of knowing how they worked or behaved in office. But every year Menon accepted my staff report, save in the case of these two women. When I left, he promoted them over the heads of others. Both these women were members of the Communist Party. Other heads of department told me that they had similar experience. ! Was Menon corrupt ? Personally never. But many of his friends to whom he entrusted the government's money were manifestly so. And he did not hesitate to take money from dubious characters for the India League and its many satellite organizations. During Menon’s tenure as High Commissioner the League and its offsprings acquired valuable Teal estate in the heart of London. Standing by old friends was a strong trait in Menon’s character. Thus he had befriended a humble cook from Malabar who bore the same name. Despite adverse reports against him, he was put in charge of India House cooking with the high sounding title “Canteen Officer”, This Menon was given to the bottle—and the number of bottles he consumed kept him chronically in the red. He played ducks and drakes with the Canteen money and on more than one occasiqn staggered into office in q state of intoxication. (At a cocktail party given to a visiting ambassador, Menon the cook gave the Ambassador’s wife a friendly pinch on her bottom.) He was often reprimanded, but not fired till after Menon ceased to be High Commissioner. Affairs of the India League and its branch organizations could very well do with some scrutiny. LIFE WITH GIANTS ECONOMICUS , ; E CONOMIC theory has long been the favourite hunting ground of the j mathematician, in his lighter moments. There is a certain aesthetic charm about marginal cost and and revenue curves, indifference maps and model building quite apart from the fact that geometry and calculus bestow on this science a certain illusory accuracy which it badly needs, Everybody has known all the time that men, firms or prices do not behave quite in this well disciplined manner. It has been pointed out time and again, and readily enough conceded, that economic variables behave with the abandon of beatniks and hippies. Nevertheless the orderly world of representative firms and gimlet-eyed entrepreneurs who continue un- failingly to bring marginal costs in line with marginal revenues and thus maximize profits still looks solid enough beyond the disorderly fringes. Or, did, until the appearance of John Kenneth Galbraith’s book The New Industrial State (Houghton Mifflin Co., Boston. Price : $6.95). The modern corporation, says Galbraith, does not maximize profit; it neither buys nor sells in a competitive market; it cannot take consumer demand for granted, neither can it afford to allow the demand to take its own course ; the state while paying lip service to anti-trust legislation allows or even neourages the large corporation to thrive by tailoring its economic and | policies to the needs of the corporation ; the stock-holders no longer d any effective power over the appointment of the management nor eem particularly anxious to want to do so. For, in general, large corporation has acquitted itself well and neither the stock- ler nor anyone else seriously wants to queer its pitch merely because ieclines to conform to the economist’s model of a typical firm ! do the Galbraith’s latest book begins with a sparkling, charmingly witty > i: the rest of the book lives up to the foreword. The book, not »r volume to “The Affluent Society” but a parent born after its ring, explores the world of giant corporations. The big corporations have made it necessary for us to revise many of our most firmly entrench- ed ideas in the field of economics. Everything Galbraith has said may be brand new but what was merely hinted as an occasional incon- venience has now been pieced together into an integrated theory. The total effect is startling. During the last 70 years there have been important changes in the industrial scene. The big corporations, no longer confined to oil, petrol- eum utilities, mining, etc, are now operating and producing all manner of products. Five hundred of the largest corporations produce half of the United States’ total goods and services. These corporations are no longer run by Fords and Carnegies. Their Chairmen are unknown people. 21

There has been a decline in the power of the ordinary stock-holder since the stock is very widely dispersed. ‘The real power rests with what Galbraith describes as the ‘techno- structure’ which consists of executives, administrative heads, scientists, engineers, salesmen and other experts along with the Board of Directors itself. It is the groups of committees and sub-committees into which these experts form themselves that take the real decisions that matter ‘such as whether to launch a new model of a car or an aeroplane, A major project takes anything from 2/3 years to complete. The corpora- tion cannot allow the product to be put at the mercy of unbridled market forces when a billion dollars have been spent in the new design and its launching. The market forces must be controlled and bent so that the model can be launched, otherwise all the expenditure and effort would be wasted. This requires extensive research and advance planning not only in the corporation but on the part of the State as well. Leaving projects of this nature to their fate is not in the interest of any one includ- ing the society and the State. Irrespective of the existing anti-Trust legislation, etc. Galbraith, therefore, comes to the conclusion that the actual conditions prevailing in the United States support the existence and development of large corporations rather than hinder it. To the three classical factors of production, land, labour and capital Knight and others added a fourth, viz., entrepreneurship, a few years ago. With the emergence of thé big corporations there is a fifth factor which ‘must be taken into account to explain what is happening in the economy. Modern technology has its own inflexible logic: a country may choose not to produce jet aircraft, nuclear power plants or even modern automobiles but it must not ask that these products —products which are the end-results of highly refined and complicated technology—be produced by firms which are subject to unfixed prices and unmanaged demand. A Pigo Galbraith, in the last chapters of his book records all this damage to eco- nomic welfare—this disregard for the marginal social product, in his inimitable style, caustic, concise, witty. Some of the stuff should ultimately achieve the status of aphorism : “Men of conservative temperament have long suspected that one thing leads to another” ; “A passenger in even a fast moving automobile is reasonably certain of keeping with it” ; “with no views is it so pleasant to agree in detail as with one’s own. . . .” For a book so refreshing and alive “The New Industrial State” has an excessive number of rather obscure passages. At times the strain of keeping pace with the author is considerable—the author is almost deter- mined not to let the reader have it too easy. The chapters dealing with the relationship between modern business and the academic and Scientific world appear like a graft which has not taken and somehow mar the unity of an undoubted classic. What Galbraith has to say about Indian planning he has said else. where (“Economic Development”, “Economic Planning in India”, ete.). Here, his harsh comments on excessive parliamentary control, belief in official omnipotence, ete., are briefly assigned to Chapter IX “A Digression on Socialism”. Any serious attempt to apply"thé Galbraith thesis to the Indian economy as such is likely to result in a degree of frustration, There is an unbridegeable gulf between the U.S. and the low-saving, i-planning Indian economy. The dissimilarities greatly outnumber the points of concurrence, The share of the public sector is of a comparable order of magnitude but that is about all. The process of arriving at a point as distinct from the location is im- nt in economics. The public sector in India has assumed its present ot as a result of the dynamics of natural growth but out of ideological ction and conscious effort. It has its economic roots somewhat un- anchored in the ground while in the absence of both the spur etition and freedom from parliamentary control the trunk and branches appear ill nourished and stunted. Whether in economic or ational matters the U.S. has always started with a policy of non- intervention and ended up with arute involvement. The result has been ind large good. OPINION, January 26, 1971 The nation state type now dominates the world, in practice as well as in theory, and the more successful of these national States are those that exhibit qualities of homogeniety and cohesiveness, discipline and aggressiye- ness. Modernizing the economy and, making planned progress in under- developed countries involves not only the building up of the appropriate structure of socio-economic institutions but also the transformation of these countries into something like nation states. A .The qualities required in a nation state or a modern developing coun- try are usually absent in the under-developed areas of the world. This is fully examplified by the case of India. Modern India was not, except under colonial rule, a single unit of administration or political organisa- tion. It has characteristics of a continent, is divided into many linguistic regions and has peoples of different faiths and ethnic groups living at widely separated levels of development of culture. The older organisation of Indian society provided for a general loose frame into which groups and communities could live at peace with others but with no compulsive movement towards integration with them. In such a society an immigrant group could settle and live and prosper in peace for centuries together without losing its identity of merging with the general community. In such a context the term general community had little significance. The society was a complex of specific communities or groups living in well- understood traditional relations with each other. Cohesion was strong within each group but there was little emphasis on the identity or cohesive- ness of society as a whole. Such an organisation though well adapted to the needs of earlier times and making for ‘survival is obviously not suitable in modern conditions. In this context it may be useful to recall Myrdal’s statement regard- n States being “soft”. The criticism of Myrdal is perfectly valid ense that it is true that Asian States are unable to take firm, iplined action in ‘given directions even when leaders are con- ( such action is appropriate. This phenomenon has to be con- nected with characteristics which Asian States derive from the composi- ind structure of their societies. Imposition of discipline and resolute iction imply a degree of cohesiveness and readiness among different social I ‘ata to identify themselves with the general social good and n these societies. It has been indicated by keen observers cy as it functions in India is too free. This again is related- ing in lae that democer to the inability of anybody. to enforce discipline. In a loosely organised society with numerous separate groupings and divided loyalties, attempts to impose rigour or discipline may lead, it is feared, to disintegration. The older societies which were tolerant and hospitable and possibly because of the virtue of non-cohesiveness were nonaggressive, today prove anachronistic, They have to be replaced by cohesive nation States which are disciplined and in which enthusiasm for working towards common ends can be built up. They must acquire the attributes of dynamism and efficiency. These are extremely important in planned economic develop- ment. Planning requires common acceptance of distant goals and ends,

OPINION, January 26, 1971 union. He once told Sheikh Abdulla, when the latter came to meet him at Wardha, “It is spirituality and not politics which would lead toa - satisfactory solution. .. Kashmir has been an integral part of India for a long time. A solution for the future of Kashmir must therefore be found within the framework of the Indian Constitution. Any attempt to separate Kashmir from the Indian Union will have serious repercussions throughout the country.” He once enquired of Nehru whether some loose confederation between India and Pakistan could be contemplated. If this is achieved, Vinoba asserted, the Kashmir problem would get automatic- ally solved. But the obvious fact is that the mutual suspicion and fears of the two countries and the hostility of Pakistan make any talk of “confederation” unrealistic, Further, it may only strengthen Pakistan’s irrational fears of India and thus instead of taking us any nearer the solution of Kashmir, it would only aggravate the tensions between the two countries. But Vinoba of course does not seriously believe that there is any real : hostility or fear between the two nations. This seems obvious from the following incident narrated by Shriman Narayan: “During his tour in Kashmir Vinoba walked on several occasions very near the cease-fire line where Indian troops were guarding the borders day and night, While he appreciated the patriotism and loyalty of these Jawans, he felt sorry that the Indian troops deployed all along the line had to idle away their time simply because of mutual fear and suspicion between India and Pakistan. On the other side of the cease-fire line could be seen the Pakistani troops similarly patrolling the borders all the twenty-four hours. When somebody pointed out to Vinoba a white jeep with the inscription ‘United Nations’ he remarked: ‘And so here is a third lot of idle men. What a large number of idle people have gathered together near the cease-fire line’.” [A saint? Maybe but of the type whose prescriptions can only be effective when the kingdom of God has taken over the earth, not when the Devil is still fighting hard for dominance and has to be kept at bay by ordinary human beings. One simple practical measure like holding the population would mean much more for the progress of the country and the happiness of the people than all the mirages our attractive visionaries, even those who habitually use simple language and down-to- earth images, pondep over and describe at length—Ed.]

BENGAL AND INDIRA V cn in Bengal has become so common that it no longer seems to merit even striking headlines in the spapers. Three, six, eight ordinary citizens wounde i every day, policemen, officials, dignitaries, stabbed, bombed, butchered in the public streets or in their own houses, has become daily routine. The news item, not too prominent, is just glanced at by the newspaper reader in other parts of the country, with at most a sigh and an ‘Oh Calcutta or Tch Bengal’, instead of the burning indignation of earlier days. There could perhaps be no greater tribute than this to the over-all managing skill of Mrs. Indira Gandhi. She has reduced in the public mind the outrageously horrible to the utterly commonplace. Directly responsible fer the government of Bengal, she has failed so completely in the most elementary, duty of any government anywhere, the maintenance of law and order, that her regime may rightly be called ‘The Intentional Mis-government of Bengal.’ At tremendous cost to the people, not’ only of Bengal, but of the country as a whole since Bengal’s industrial establish- ments and raw produce serve the whole country, she has kept the Com- munists happy. Their true representative, the egregious Dhavan, still continues her chosen and cherished Governor. To move him, to take the really stern measures demanded by the ‘near-civil-war situation, would mean displeasing not only her Communist supporters here but also in- curring the anger of the Soviet Communist leaders, and that to her is- of course uLthinkable. Even if all her other sins of commission and omission were forgiven Mrs. Indira Gandhi, her conscious mishandling of the Bengal situation alone is enough to damn her. That after it she should continue to be Prime Minister, is proof of the poor quality, lack of spirit and self of so many of our legislators. \ THE LESSON OF CHILE F you want to know how the softening-up process of the Communists works and what it results in, take a look at Chile, where the Com- munists have come to power through a popular front and a Communist president is now Doplying Communist doctrine to free institutions. For years, the Communists have been working away strengthening their hold in societies, clubs, professional associations, trade unions, newspapers, etc., pretending to be reasonable, just like any other Party in fact. As with our own CPI, people began to think of the Communists as not too extreme really, men one could get along with. And so the via pacifica, the peace- ful way, paid off, and Salvador Allende is now President, with the clear intention of turning Chile into a ‘People’s’ Democracy on the well-known Russian model. Thus does quiet penetration bring its reward, oh gullible Indians! Allende's coalition had only thirty-six per cent of the vote, but the other parties instead of joining up against it, continued with their 3

4 8 - OPINION, December 29, 1970 own differences and allowed him to creep in. And now the repenting has begun, but of what use can it be? Allow Communist power to be estab- lished once, the instruments of state sanction to pass into Communist control, and in modern conditions all hope of a return to freedom must be vain. Behind the local Communist or Communist-dominated Govern- ment stands also the Communist Soviet Union. Soviet money, Soviet arms, Soviet guidance through diplomats and intelligence agents, all are easily available to the local Government in need. And why not, ‘since the Communist leaders of such countries kneel to do reverence to the Soviet Communist leaders on the necks of their own countrymen? It takes a very long spoon to sup with the Devil in safety, friends; those who accept his cordial invitations invariably end up as part of his feast. Beware, while there is still time. Soon, it may be too late. ` DIEGO GARCIAS AND ARMS TO SOUTH AFRICA T is as foolish for the Indian Government to object to the Diego Garcias scheme for the establishment of a/staging centre in the Indian Ocean by the British and Americans as it is for the British Government to persist in wanting to give arms to South Africa. Indian interests are not served by the objection just as British interests are not served by the supply. The Soviet Union is building up substantial naval strength in the Indian Ocean, and there is no sense in keeping on saying “oh but the Indian ocean must be kept free from the intrusion of the great powers.” Who has the strength to keep it free? Certainly none of the countries whose shores it touches, nor even a. combination of all of them. Surely then it is better that the Soviet presence alone should not dominate the area, that countervailing forces to it should also be readily available. British and American forces in the Indian ocean may help to prevent Soviet interference in, and subjection of, some of the countries whose shores are washed by it. The great powers on both sides will constantly be watching one another, with the result that conditions may be much better for the less powerful countries than if the only real force in the Ocean was that of the Soviet Union. Turning to the British government’s proposal to help- South Africa, it may be noted that even the American Governmekt, interested as it cannot but be in the Soviet extension of power to the Indian Ocean, sees no merit in it. If persisted in, it will be a singular exhibition of obstinacy on the part of a Government from which its people no less than the rest of the democratic world, have a right to expect common-sense and reasonable behaviour. A large section of opinion in Britain may have come round to the view that the Commonwealth no longer serves any purpose and had better be dissolved, but surely there could be better ways of dissolving it, if that is the intention—parting as friends by common agreement for instance—than by establishing Britain in the world’s mind as the backer of apartheid and blatant racial superiority.

But what if he wanted to draw out money against it in a day or two? Oh well, there-could be no question of that, since the bank was just not clearing cheques at all. The writer stood around helplessly, cheque in hand. Said a kindly fellow account-holder, clearly a man of experience and worldly wisdom, “You know in these days it is always good to keep at home a few thousand rupees to meet sudden emergencies like this. You really can't rely upon our banks any more. At a moment's notice, work may stop. Supposing the Manager in that cabin were to come out and ask those two there, before whom a crowd is standing, to stop talking and get on with the work, the whole lot might down pens and walk out. The banks, they tell you if you grumble at the delay, are nationalised, perhaps you have not heard, so in due course, in due course.” The writer wondered if he should follow the advice, but where would he keep any large sum, he thought, accustomed as he is to having only a couple of hundred around at a time. He recollected too that only that morning Indiraji had descanted on the great benefit bank nationalisation had conferred on sections of society such as taxi and rickshaw drivers. Well in this wonderful country of ours there's never any lack of something to be cheerful about, he reflected with a smile.

OPINION, December 29, 1970 There is a mad scramble for power by the Global-Powers all over the world. Nonetheless, smaller countries can and should maintain their inde- pendence. They must not yield to the Global Powers, for to do so would be a “negation of the struggle of man, expressed through the nation state, to be free”. It is possible for the smaller countries with adroit handling ‚of their affairs to maintain their independence. The Bhutto recipe reads as follows : rae “It would be inexpedient, and perhaps dangerous, for smaller nations to identify themselves completely with the total interests of one Global Power to the exclusion of the others. Common interest and the pattern of events may make it necessary for a small nation to be more closely associated with one Global Power than with another, but, even so, it is not impossible for it to maintain normal relations with the others on the basis of honourable bilateral relations. When the national interests of a state clash with the interests of a Global Power, it would be preferable to isolate the area of conflict in the direct dealings with that Great Power. A workable equilibrium should be sought independent of the point on which vital interests differ, provided, of course, that the segregation of conflicting interests is not only possible but is scrupulously ~ reciprocal. Every reasonable effort should be made to put into action preventive diplomacy to avoid Global Power interventions which subject the weaker nations to suffer from punitive diplomacy. If this, however, is not found to be feasible, it is better to make the position clear by taking a stand against encroachment. It is preferable to have one sharp crisis and a firm position than to permit procrastination to create conditions of per- manent crises. In such a situation, every subsequent crisis will do greater harm to the smaller Power until eventually the Global Power overwhelms it. So, if insulation is not possible, it is better to take a positive position and evolve a new pattern of understanding. Pressure is both a worm and a monster. It is a worm if you stamp on it, but becomes a monster if you recoil.” Two ideas lie at the rest of this policy. One is bilateralism in rela- tionship and the other is the theory of isolation. Prevent points of differ- ence affecting the relationship by an agreement to differ. “It would provide us with an opportunity for normal relations with all states, yet be reconcilable with the active pursuit of our objectives. It would give us freedom to pursue our legitimate objectives without fear ‚of inimical foreign intervention, and would not prevent us from endeavour- ing by indirect influences and persuasion to bring about favourable changes in the attitude of those Powers which are either hostile or neutral. There is a fundamental difference between “pre-conditions for normal relations and ‘persuasion’ without preconditions. By not seeking intervention for the resolution of our disputes, we would not be prevented from trying to persuade other countries to take a right position. It goes without saying that, if a state were to change its position voluntarily on account of the application of indirect pressure, or for other reasons, there would be a corresponding change in our bilateral relations with that state,” .

RAO T: is a curious situation that political parties with leaders of undoubt repute and character should place dubious candidates before ti electorate on the ground that better qualified candidates have no chane of success, while many an elector should grumble that the alternatiy open to him are equally bleak. The point is that organisational changes may speed up. procedure. They can be of help in bringing cases to decision; but they cannot by themselves compel a deciding authority to take a decision. Procrastination of decisions for political reasons can only be avoided by leaders who are prepared to lead. In 1956, in connection with the extensive reorganisations then in the offing, a number of ministers from various States had gathered together. The discussion somehow strayed into the educational and professional Ae. complishments of the leaders in power who had foregathered at the meet- ing. Minister after minister took pride in relating his poor achievements in school and college and of his equally poor performance in his sub- sequent attempts to establish himself in a profession. Success apparently came their way only after they decided to switch their attention to poli- tics. Two of the ministers present were almost apologetic for the successes they had achieved both in their educational and professional careers. Second chambers, available at the Centre and in many States, do provide a ready means of securing the services of people of talent who may not be willing, or able, to rough it out at the hustings. The BHIKSHU K. and The Lady Abbess SNEHLATA DAMYANTI ES, yes it’s indisputably getting colder and soon we will come round to that otherwise beautiful time of the year when the great myth of the gentle saint will be raised. Of how He played simple-mindedly with children, and gently but drolly turned his head from side to side to exhibit now one cheek and now the other. Some of us will be aware a little uncomfortably of His boot on the backside of the money changers and of his great friendship with certain innkeepers and popsies. ‘As above so below’ said His Guru’s Guru. Nevertheless we will gaze raptly and joyously at the glowing halo around His head but will gloss quickly over what we fondly imagine to be solid polished expensive marble, waist downwards. Ask no questions and if you do, avert your eyes! So it will in no wise profit us if we are told the truth, that yes indeed He was the Son of God but also that he was an Essene and bathed with less than great regularity and therefore scratched frequently in a manner that would now be considered offensive. If in addition we were informed that he had real genitalia, that worked (or worse still that He actually used them) we would be filled with such shame, abhorrence and disgust, that we would soon cease to revere the Sons of God, leave alone wish to imitate or be like them. No, no, it will have to be put quite differently. Truth disguised as a fairy story which happens to be true. When the Arahat Angulimala was old and greying in a wickedly dis- tinguished manner (indeed he still retained the hawk nose and piercing eye that were his as the greatest bandit of his time. He had grown gentle with the years, even though he still chewed raw meat, and pulled method- ically at his underarm hair as he rocked back and forth, nursing old scars and recalling his Enlightenment experience.
